    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1159 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Krebsonsecurity ↗ Open Full Page

    Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a tech giant that helps websites customize user experiences and test out upcoming features.
    • Sources indicate that the Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely.
    • Industry observers note that helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a tech giant that helps websites customize user experiences and test out upcoming features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

    Sources indicate that the Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

    Industry observers note that helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

    According to recent reports, “The vital lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”.

    Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”.

    “We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”.

    According to recent reports, many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

    It has been revealed that one reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely indicates, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

    It has been revealed that zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is crucial since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

    Sources indicate that “So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he mentioned. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”.

    Recent findings suggest that websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

    “With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, upcoming domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he mentioned. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”.

    How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The manufacturer found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

    The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security complications. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected consumers, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

    Helme remarked he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

    Recent findings suggest that “Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme mentioned in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”.

    Sources indicate that internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each fresh website.

    Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end consumers was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

    Recent findings suggest that upgrade, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

    #137955. CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1489 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Krebsonsecurity ↗ Open Full Page

    CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1489 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
    • A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.
    • The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

    A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

    The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

    “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”.

    But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the firm’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

    Industry observers note that the indictment states the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim organization and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

    In a recent development, the government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim tech giant that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

    According to recent reports, the following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

    According to recent reports, paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

    Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”.

    Industry observers note that A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

    The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”.

    “Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

    According to recent reports, ihme mentioned RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the firm could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

    Recent findings suggest that A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

    It has been revealed that but Ihme noted a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

    Sources indicate that A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

    According to recent reports, “The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme remarked. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”.

    According to recent reports, indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit rapidly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

    Industry observers note that the Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

    In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

    According to recent reports, “The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”.

    The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a latest negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

    In a recent development, “I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”.

    Sources indicate that ihme mentioned RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

    “If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme mentioned. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

    Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

    In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

    Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (463 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license.
    • audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.
    • Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

    audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

    Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

    Recent findings suggest that to find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

    It has been revealed that on-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

    Sources indicate that on the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

    Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

    Sources indicate that clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

    It has been revealed that the weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

    Industry observers note that we're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

    This Breakfast Addition Sharpens Memory Later In The Day

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.

    A generous handful produced small cognitive benefits over the following six hours, although memory performance varied with the timing of the tests.

    Walnuts may influence how the brain directs attention and obtains the energy needed for demanding mental work.

    Professor Claire Williams, study co-author, said:.

    “A handful of walnuts with breakfast could give young adults a mental edge when they need to perform at the top of their game.”.

    The research involved over 30 healthy young adults aged 18–30, who ate two different breakfasts on separate visits to the laboratory.

    One contained 50 g of crushed walnuts mixed into muesli and vanilla yoghurt, while the other contained no nuts.

    The breakfasts contained almost identical calorie and fat totals, with butter added to the comparison meal to help achieve this match.

    Participants completed tests before breakfast and again two, four and six hours afterwards, while researchers also recorded their brain activity.

    After the walnut breakfast, participants responded faster on tasks involving attention, resisting distractions and switching between different mental rules.

    These abilities form part of executive function, which helps us control our responses and adapt to changing demands.

    The differences were modest, averaging around eight milliseconds on the attention test and 22 milliseconds when switching between rules.

    Whether improvements of this size would make a noticeable difference outside the laboratory remains uncertain.

    The memory findings were more complicated.

    Two hours after eating walnuts, participants performed slightly worse when repeatedly learning and recalling a list of words.

    By six hours, however, the pattern had reversed, with better performance after walnuts than after the comparison breakfast.

    One possibility is that walnuts helped protect learning performance as the testing day wore on.

    Repeated mental effort can make it harder to take in latest information, so preserving the ability to learn could be useful even without improving every aspect of memory.

    However, participants did not report feeling less mentally fatigued after walnuts, leaving this explanation unconfirmed.

    Another possibility is that some benefits emerged gradually as nutrients were absorbed and processed.

    Walnuts contain omega-3 fats, protein and plant compounds called polyphenols, which could contribute individually or together.

    Electrical recordings revealed differences in frontal and parietal brain activity after the two breakfasts.

    These regions contribute to attention, memory and the control of behaviour.

    The changes may indicate that walnuts altered how mental resources were allocated during the tests, although they do not establish precisely why performance improved.

    Blood samples also showed slightly higher glucose availability and lower concentrations of circulating free fatty acids after walnuts.

    Greater glucose availability might help fuel demanding mental work.

    The study was published in the journal Food & Function (Bell et al., 2025).

    Sources indicate that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Are you looking for a newly introduced graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free. Let's start the review.

    Canva has a web version and also a mobile app.

    Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson aims, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

    Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

    Industry observers note that to create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

    Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

    So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

    The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

    It has been revealed that to get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large firm, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

    Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

    According to recent reports, next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

    You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

    Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

    To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:.

    The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

    If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

    It has been revealed that with Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

    With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

    Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

    It has been revealed that the Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

    In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

    Sources indicate that in general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors.     180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.
    • Recent findings suggest that I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.
    • According to recent reports, orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

    Recent findings suggest that I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

    According to recent reports, orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

    I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

    My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

    When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

    Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

    It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

    Sources indicate that that's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

    Industry observers note that before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

    It has been revealed that llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

    Sources indicate that vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's major batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

    Sources indicate that transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

    I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:.

    Industry observers note that offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

    It has been revealed that if the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

    Sources indicate that strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

    In a recent development, all of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

    I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

    Recent findings suggest that first version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

    Sources indicate that the fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

    Sources indicate that I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:.

    Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:.

    That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

    Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

    According to recent reports, the API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization blueprint of #50245 rather than their own option.

    Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:.

    Sources indicate that the conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

    Recent findings suggest that the model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

    Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:.

    Industry observers note that strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

    Recent findings suggest that I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

    Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:.

    Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:.

    These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:.

    That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

    Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

    It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

    Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

    Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

    Sources indicate that the generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

    Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

    #137949. 5 MySQL EXPLAIN Signals That Tell You Exactly Why Your Query Is Slow

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (521 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    5 MySQL EXPLAIN Signals That Tell You Exactly Why Your Query Is Slow

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that most slow MySQL queries announce themselves if you know where to look.
    • MySQL read every row of the table no matter what your WHERE said.
    • According to recent reports, different from signal 1 in one notable way: sometimes possible_keys lists an index and key is still NULL.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that most slow MySQL queries announce themselves if you know where to look. You do not need a monitoring dashboard or a database consultant — you need EXPLAIN, and five signals in its output that each point at a different fix.

    This is the loudest signal. MySQL read every row of the table no matter what your WHERE said. On a lookup table with 50 rows, nobody cares. On a table with 500,000 rows, this is your whole problem. The fix is almost always an index on the column in the WHERE clause. Run the query again after adding it and watch type move to ref.

    According to recent reports, different from signal 1 in one notable way: sometimes possible_keys lists an index and key is still NULL. That means the index exists and MySQL refused it. The usual reason is the query itself — a function wrapped around the indexed column, like DATE(created_at) = '2026-11-20', or a comparison against a value of the wrong type. Rewrite the condition so the index can serve it: a date range instead of DATE(), matching types on both sides.

    The index found the rows, but they came back in the wrong order, so MySQL sorted them itself — in memory if it fits, on disk if it does not. The cure is a composite index that covers the filter and the sort in one order: equality columns first, then the sort column. An index on (user_id, created_at) serves WHERE user_id = 1234 ORDER BY created_at DESC with no sort at all — MySQL reads the index backwards and stops after your LIMIT.

    Industry observers note that rows is an estimate, not a count, but the ratio tells the story. If MySQL expects to examine 498,000 rows to hand you back 20, the plan is wrong even if the query eventually finishes. Compare rows with the actual result size. A ratio in the thousands means a missing index or a condition the optimizer cannot use. When the estimate itself looks suspicious, EXPLAIN ANALYZE (MySQL 8.0.18+) runs the query and reports the real numbers.

    Recent findings suggest that this one does not show up as a single bad column — it highlights up as a query that is fast on page 1 and slow on page 1,000. LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20000 still reads and discards 20,000 rows. The fix is keyset pagination: remember the last id you showed and ask for the next rows after it with WHERE id > 20000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20. The index does the work, and page 1,000 costs the same as page 1.

    None of these signals needs a rewrite of your application. The habit is small: when a query is slow, run EXPLAIN before you change anything, read these five signals, and make the smallest change that moves one of them. I wrote up the full walkthrough — finding the slow queries in the slow query log, reading every column, and verifying each fix — here:.

    https://rajadevsolutions.online/blog/how-to-fix-slow-mysql-queries-with-explain.

    Industry observers note that fix the proposal first. The query is usually innocent.

    #137947. Industry News: 21 of My 50 Austin Homes Had No Days on Market. All 21 Were Compass 'Early Access' Listings

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (862 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: 21 of My 50 Austin Homes Had No Days on Market. All 21 Were Compass 'Early Access' Listings

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that I run a visa agency in Bali, and in the evenings I build data tools on Apify.
    • The actor gets checked on a schedule with the input a new user sees first:.
    • I had eight of those runs from 20 to 22 November 2026, each 50 homes, each finished in 2.7 to 4.3 seconds.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I run a visa agency in Bali, and in the evenings I build data tools on Apify. One of them is a Redfin Scraper. You type a place the way you'd type it into Redfin's search box (Austin, TX, 78704, Travis County, TX) or paste a Redfin search URL, pick for sale, sold or for rent, and get one flat row per home: price, beds, baths, square feet, lot size, year built, coordinates, days on market, MLS number, HOA and the main photo.

    The actor gets checked on a schedule with the input a new user sees first:.

    I had eight of those runs from 20 to 22 November 2026, each 50 homes, each finished in 2.7 to 4.3 seconds. I opened the latest dataset to check the fields, and the first thing I noticed was how many rows were missing daysOnMarket. It was 21 of 50.

    They weren't random gaps. Every one of the 21 had status: "Coming Soon" and isComingSoon: true, and every one carried the same two badges:.

    Sources indicate that the other 29 rows were ordinary active listings with badges like For Sale and 3D Walkthrough. None of them had a Compass badge.

    So with Redfin's default "recommended" order, 42% of the first page in Austin was one brokerage's pre-market inventory. The share held up across all eight runs: 21, 21, 21, 21, 23, 23, 22, 23. And it isn't a one-off ordering quirk. 45 property IDs demonstrated up in all eight runs, and only 55 distinct homes appeared in total.

    This is a real Coming Soon row from the 22 November run (description left out):.

    No price. No pricePerSqft. No daysOnMarket, listedAt, hoa or redfinAgentName. I counted across all 21 Coming Soon rows in that run:.

    * HOA is genuinely absent for many houses, so I only note that no Coming Soon row had one.

    In a recent development, the mlsId isn't an MLS number you can look up. Every active row in Austin had a 7-digit id like 4729441 or 3953946. Every Coming Soon row had a 19-digit one like 2240202255479679921. Same field, same API, different source. The photo URLs follow the same split: photo/92/bigphoto/946/3953946_0.jpg for an active home and photo/641/bigphoto/921/2240202255479679921_0.jpg for a Coming Soon one. If you're joining Redfin rows to an MLS feed by mlsId, those 21 rows won't match anything, and that isn't a parsing bug.

    They're more expensive. Among the 16 Coming Soon rows that did have a price, the median was $700,000. The 29 active rows had a median of $425,000. One house sitting near the top of the Coming Soon list was a 5,518 sq ft place on 1.63 acres.

    The usual first experiment with a real-estate scraper is to pull 50 homes and compute something: median price, average days on market, share of condos. With the default settings on this search, each of those numbers comes out skewed in a predictable direction:.

    None of this is wrong data. Redfin demonstrates Coming Soon homes in its own search by default, and the actor does the same so the output matches what you see in the browser. But it's a different kind of record, and treating it the same as an active listing breaks the arithmetic.

    Turn it off at the source. The input has includeComingSoon (default true). Set it to false and the search asks Redfin for active listings only. The 50 rows you pay for are then 50 homes with a price, a listing date and an agent.

    Keep it and split it. If pre-market inventory is the thing you're after (it often is for buyers' agents), keep the default and branch on the flag:.

    Industry observers note that notice the type == "home" filter. The last row of every run is a free summary row with type: "notice". In this run it said: "Run summary: 50 row(s) delivered, 0 free; charged home ×50 = $0.0165." It's useful for reconciling costs, but it isn't a home. Switch it off with includeRunSummary: false if your pipeline can't skip it.

    Industry observers note that while comparing the eight runs I found that one condo had eight slightly different listedAt values: from 2026-11-12T15:15:30.866Z to 2026-11-12T15:15:31.154Z. 29 of the 30 live listings that had a listedAt demonstrated more than one value across runs.

    That one's on my side. Redfin's search response doesn't send a listing timestamp. It sends how long the home has been on Redfin, in milliseconds. The actor subtracts that from the moment it reads the page, so the result moves by a few hundred milliseconds from run to run. It's accurate to the second, but it isn't a stable key. If you dedupe across runs, use propertyId plus listingId. Don't use listedAt.

    A few things I learned building this that apply whether you use my actor or write your own:.

    If you just want "what's for sale in this ZIP right now, as a spreadsheet", the default input does that. Just decide before you calculate anything whether Coming Soon homes belong in your numbers. In Austin this week they were 21 of the 50.

    The actor is here: Redfin Scraper on Apify.

    Latest Update: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
    • Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
    • Industry observers note that the challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

    Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

    Industry observers note that the challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

    IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

    In a recent development, foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to latest series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

    It has been revealed that figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

    Industry observers note that now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

    The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

    See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

    Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that upgrade at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

    A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

    In a recent development, figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

    According to recent reports, time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

    Sources indicate that figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

    This approach can help teams in four ways:.

    Recent findings suggest that -Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

    Recent findings suggest that -Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

    Sources indicate that -Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

    It has been revealed that -Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

    It has been revealed that figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

    The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

    An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a latest cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

    Recent findings suggest that to get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

    When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

    According to recent reports, the outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

    Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

    In a recent development, A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

    AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each latest reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

    Recent findings suggest that when sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

    Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

    A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

    In a recent development, with AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as latest sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

    When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

    In a recent development, figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

    According to recent reports, fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

    In a recent development, A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

    The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

    Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

    An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

    On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

    According to recent reports, if a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

    Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

    A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

    Recent findings suggest that TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

    In a recent development, this application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

    Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

    The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:.

    Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A latest cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

    Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

    Recent findings suggest that banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

    Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

    In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

    The Urgency of Early ADHD Intervention

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that delaying treatment for ADHD until the teen years comes with potential life-long consequences.
    • Q: I believe my elementary school-age child has ADHD, but my husband doesn’t think so.
    • Sources indicate that this question reflects a dilemma faced by many families: What happens when one parent wants possible signs of ADHD evaluated while another prefers to wait and see?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that delaying treatment for ADHD until the teen years comes with potential life-long consequences. Here’s what you should know.

    Q: I believe my elementary school-age child has ADHD, but my husband doesn’t think so. He refuses to get our child evaluated. I have ADHD and I know this can run in families. What should I do?

    Sources indicate that this question reflects a dilemma faced by many families: What happens when one parent wants possible signs of ADHD evaluated while another prefers to wait and see? The answer may matter more than many people realize.

    Imagine two children entering first grade:.

    According to recent reports, jacob is bright, curious, and energetic. He struggles to sit still, frequently forgets to turn in his homework, and has difficulty following multi-step instructions. His teacher notices the symptoms and relays these to his parents. Jacob’s pediatrician conducts a comprehensive evaluation and diagnoses Jacob with ADHD.

    According to recent reports, his parents learn strategies to support him at home. His school implements accommodations. Later, medication becomes part of his treatment blueprint. Jacob still faces challenges, but he learns how his brain works and develops tools to succeed. He graduates from high school with strong grades and heads off to college.

    [Webinar Replay: “6 Principles for Raising a Child with ADHD”].

    Now imagine Maya. She is also intelligent, but her suspected ADHD symptoms present differently. She daydreams in class and quietly falls behind. She is emotionally sensitive, often taking criticism to heart and becoming overwhelmed by setbacks that her peers seem to brush off. Her teachers describe her as capable but inconsistent. Because she isn’t disruptive, her struggles are attributed to a lack of effort, disorganization, anxiety, or immaturity.

    Year after year, she works harder while feeling increasingly frustrated. As academic demands increase, so do her feelings of self-doubt and inadequacy. By the time she receives an ADHD diagnosis at age 16, her grades have suffered, her confidence has eroded, and she is considering leaving school altogether.

    The paths of these two children, one who received early intervention with medication and one who remained untreated until her mid-teens, illustrate a growing concern in ADHD care: It’s not simply about whether children are diagnosed, but when.

    [Self-Test: Could Your Preschooler Have ADHD?].

    Sources indicate that A recent study published in JAMA Psychiatry examined educational outcomes among more than 580,000 individuals with ADHD. The researchers found that children diagnosed earlier in life had significantly better educational outcomes than those diagnosed during adolescence. Earlier diagnosis with associated with higher grade point averages, a greater likelihood of pursuing academic educational tracks, and substantially lower rates of school dropout.

    The differences were striking. Individuals diagnosed during the early elementary school years had school dropout rates of approximately 9 percent by age 20, compared with nearly 30 percent among those first diagnosed around age 16. Similar patterns were observed in both males and females. The researchers concluded that adolescents diagnosed later represent a particularly vulnerable group.

    Industry observers note that the findings do not suggest that a diagnosis alone changes a child’s future. Rather, earlier recognition creates opportunities for intervention. Children identified sooner can access school accommodations, behavioral supports, parent education, and, when appropriate, medication – before years of academic struggles, self-doubt, and declining confidence take hold and begin to shape their identity.

    This raises an important question: How many Mayas are sitting in classrooms today, struggling silently while waiting years for recognition or a diagnosis?

    Sources indicate that universal ADHD screening offers a potential solution. Many children with ADHD are identified only after academic, social, or emotional difficulties have become impossible to ignore. Screening creates an opportunity to recognize concerns earlier before the consequences of undiagnosed ADHD begin to accumulate. Importantly, screening is not diagnosis. It is simply an invitation to look more closely.

    Many critics of universal screening worry about overdiagnosis or unnecessary labeling. Those concerns deserve consideration. However, screening itself does not determine whether a child has ADHD. It merely identifies children who may benefit from a more comprehensive evaluation, meaning that fewer children with significant challenges get overlooked.

    Growing evidence suggests that every year of delayed recognition carries educational and emotional costs that are difficult to reverse. Universal screening will not identify every child. But it may help more children find the right path before they wander too far afield.

    Industry observers note that for many children, the greatest risk may not be receiving an ADHD diagnosis. It may be never receiving one at all.

    Here are three actions that caregivers can take:.

    Agentic AI Security Framework for SMEs

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that small and mid-sized teams can secure agentic AI systems without the heavy tech stacks used by large enterprises.
    • Agentic AI goes beyond text generation, it reads context, calls tools, fetches data, and takes actions over multiple steps.
    • For small businesses, the real challenge is to let agents automate useful work without handing over too much trust, because one weak prompt, tool call, or system integration can expose sensitive data or trigger risky actions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that small and mid-sized teams can secure agentic AI systems without the heavy tech stacks used by large enterprises. The core move: treat the AI agent as untrusted, and then set clear control points around identity, permissions, data flow, and human approval. Here’s how to build a practical agentic AI security framework for SMEs that actually works day-to-day.

    Agentic AI goes beyond text generation, it reads context, calls tools, fetches data, and takes actions over multiple steps. This means greater efficiency, but also a much bigger attack surface than standard chatbots. A working agentic AI security framework doesn’t just govern what the model says; it has to gate what the agent can access, which actions are allowed, and how decisions are reviewed.

    For small businesses, the real challenge is to let agents automate useful work without handing over too much trust, because one weak prompt, tool call, or system integration can expose sensitive data or trigger risky actions.

    The main risks for SMEs tend to be the ones that show up in ordinary daily workflows:.

    These risk areas are echoed across security guides, including JetBrains’ breakdown of AI agent security and Check Point’s seven key agentic AI risks. Ignoring these in SME automation pipelines is a recipe for trouble.

    Sources indicate that you don’t need hundreds of controls or expensive software. Instead, focus on a handful of controls applied at the right touch points:.

    Sources indicate that don’t share accounts between agents or let access linger longer than needed. Give each agent only as much access as needed for a specific job. Use unique, short-lived credentials where possible. If the agent runs inside a user’s session, tie its permissions to that session and expire them quickly.

    In a recent development, don’t trust setup-time permissions alone. Check every outbound call, tool use, and data fetch as it happens. Block anything not specifically approved for that request, especially egress to outside systems.

    Keep a living spreadsheet of which agents can touch what. For each agent, list the approved tools, allowed data sources, blocked actions, responsible person, and when it was last reviewed. This lets you spot risky sprawl and cut access when a workflow changes.

    In a recent development, watch for outlier behaviors, odd tool calls, repeated retrying, or escalations to sensitive data. If something doesn’t fit the normal workflow, pause or block it. Guardrails should especially cover actions that could cause real-world damage.

    Recent findings suggest that record which prompts, user inputs, docs, or tool results led to each action. This makes post-mortems and explanations much easier, as highlighted in Uber’s guide to agentic AI security.

    According to recent reports, security is easier when it’s designed into the workflow, not added as an afterthought. Here’s a practical SME pattern:.

    SMEs already running connected websites, data pipelines, and AI automations will recognize this approach from guides like SIÁN Agency’s practical playbooks for small data teams.

    Let’s spell it out for a fictional sales automation agent:.

    Begin small: pick a workflow that saves time but won’t cause disasters if it fails. Map the data it touches, the tools it touches, and strip out all unnecessary powers. Add explicit approval for anything risky, and turn on logging from day one.

    Already running agents in production? Run a short security review specifically on permissions and data flows. Want help going from review to finished workflow? Book a call with SIÁN Agency, who specialize in stitching secure, automation-ready pipelines together for SMEs.

    Security for agentic AI isn’t just for significant tech, it’s absolutely practical for SMEs, provided you keep the framework tight, enhancement access frequently, and put humans on the loop where it counts.
