    #137941. Latest Update: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1397 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
    • In a recent development, A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
    • GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

    In a recent development, A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

    GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

    Industry observers note that better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It indicates nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

    In a recent development, we wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

    The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

    For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

    Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

    This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

    These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

    To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

    In a recent development, we treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

    Two design choices shaped the work:.

    We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

    In a recent development, distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

    Recent findings suggest that all numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

    No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

    A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That states nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It highlights how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

    Industry observers note that linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

    Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

    Sources indicate that catBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

    Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

    Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

    According to recent reports, one caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

    Recent findings suggest that looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

    Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

    In a recent development, out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

    Recent findings suggest that more data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

    In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

    Recent findings suggest that what does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

    Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

    It has been revealed that the full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

    Dharma-AI R&D · We Make AI Your Model.

    DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
    • The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
    • In a recent development, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

    The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

    The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

    In a recent development, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

    After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

    The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

    Recent findings suggest that daisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

    Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

    Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

    In a recent development, we built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

    We selected tasks using three criteria:.

    According to recent reports, radixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

    57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

    2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

    Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

    Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

    Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

    Industry observers note that our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

    In a recent development, the service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

    Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

    Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

    We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

    We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

    Tech Report: Hunt4Coin vs Freqtrade for crypto backtesting: which one should you use?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that use Hunt4Coin if you want to test a rule on one coin in a few minutes, in a browser, without writing code; use Freqtrade if you can write Python and want to test many pairs at once, optimise parameters and later run the same strategy as a bot.
    • We build Hunt4Coin, so we have a stake in this comparison.
    • In a recent development, hunt4Coin suits traders who want an answer to "would this rule have worked on this coin?" without installing anything.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that use Hunt4Coin if you want to test a rule on one coin in a few minutes, in a browser, without writing code; use Freqtrade if you can write Python and want to test many pairs at once, optimise parameters and later run the same strategy as a bot. Both are free and both include exchange fees in their results. Hunt4Coin is a free crypto charts, screener and backtesting site built by Quantumines; Freqtrade is an independent, open-source trading bot written in Python.

    We build Hunt4Coin, so we have a stake in this comparison. To keep it fair, every fact about Freqtrade below comes from its own documentation and every fact about Hunt4Coin from hunt4coin.com, both read on 23 November 2026, and we say plainly where Freqtrade is the stronger tool.

    In a recent development, hunt4Coin suits traders who want an answer to "would this rule have worked on this coin?" without installing anything. You pick a coin, a timeframe and how many candles to test, then set entry rules such as "RSI(14) crosses above 30" or "Price > EMA(200)", optional exit rules, a stop-loss and take-profit in percent, a fee per side, the position size and starting capital. Signed in with a free account, you can type the strategy in plain English instead, and the site turns it into rules and lists anything it could not express.

    It has been revealed that the result page demonstrates an equity curve, every trade, net profit, buy-and-hold for comparison, win rate, profit factor, maximum drawdown and Sharpe ratio, next to the same test without fees. It also warns when fees turn a profit into a loss.

    According to recent reports, hunt4Coin's own worked example reveals why that matters. A MACD crossover (12, 26, 9) on Bitcoin 1-hour candles from 1 August to 31 October 2026 made +14.12% before fees over 86 round trips, and lost 3.92% at 0.1% per side, because fees cost $1,817.35 on a $10,000 account. Every trade is in a downloadable CSV. That is an illustration of fees, not a strategy to copy.

    Sources indicate that freqtrade suits people who can write Python and want more control than any web form gives. Strategies are written in Python with pandas, so you can use any indicator or logic you can code. A single backtest runs across every pair in your configuration, you can compare several strategies in one run, and Hyperopt searches for the best parameters for entries, exits, ROI targets, stop-loss and trailing stop.

    The bigger difference is what happens after the test. The same strategy can run in dry-run mode with simulated money, then live on an exchange, controlled through Telegram or a web interface. Freqtrade lists Binance, Bitget, Bybit, Gate, HTX, Hyperliquid, Kraken and OKX among its supported spot exchanges. Its documentation is also frank about the risk: it calls the software educational, recommends basic coding skills and tells users to start in dry-run before risking money.

    Industry observers note that if you want a research tool that grows into an automated bot, Freqtrade is the stronger choice. Hunt4Coin deliberately stops before that point.

    According to recent reports, A backtest only sees each candle's open, high, low and close, so every tool has to assume what happened in between. These assumptions explain why two tools can show different results for the same idea.

    Neither models slippage on a market order. Hunt4Coin says it also leaves out the bid-ask spread, order-book depth, partial fills and funding costs on short positions, and suggests setting the fee a little higher to allow for them. Freqtrade's documentation says a backtest will never replace running a strategy in dry-run mode.

    No. Past candles are public, so neither tool needs your keys to backtest. Hunt4Coin never asks for API keys at all. Freqtrade downloads historical data with download-data from the exchange you name; you only add API keys when you move from dry-run to live trading. Our answer on backtesting for free without giving exchange API keys covers how to keep keys safe if you ever automate.

    Yes, and many people would benefit from it. A practical order is to sketch an idea on Hunt4Coin's charts, run a quick backtest with fees to see if it survives at all, practise it with paper trading at live prices, and only then write it as a Freqtrade strategy if you want to test it across many pairs, optimise it or automate it. Whatever the tool, past results do not predict future returns.

    According to recent reports, hunt4Coin is one of many projects at Quantumines, the product studio founded by Muhammad Ali Raza (Ali Arbi) in Lahore. For other free crypto tools, see our answer on a free crypto screener with RSI and MACD.

    In a recent development, no. Hunt4Coin is a no-code backtester for one coin at a time and never trades. Freqtrade is a programmable bot that backtests many pairs, optimises parameters and can trade live. They overlap only in the backtesting step.

    Yes. Freqtrade is free and open source. You pay only for the machine you run it on and the exchange fees on any live trades.

    Yes. Hunt4Coin uses a fee per side that you pick from a list of exchange fees and demonstrates results with and without fees. Freqtrade uses the exchange's default fee, or the one you set with --fee, on both entry and exit.

    Hunt4Coin, because it needs no install, no code and no API keys. Freqtrade's own documentation recommends basic coding skills and Python knowledge before using it.

    Hunt4Coin facts read on hunt4coin.com (its backtesting page, worked fee example and llms.txt) on 23 November 2026; Freqtrade facts from its backtesting, data downloading and home pages, read the same day. This article compares software; it is not financial advice.

    Bing fetched our site for 15 days and got zero successful pages

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (370 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that bing's crawl stats answer a question Google's console cannot: did the crawler arrive, and did it get a 200 when it did.
    • We read the numbers from the Bing Webmaster API every day on our own site.
    • Sources indicate that on 11-12 Bing fetched five URLs and got zero successful pages.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that bing's crawl stats answer a question Google's console cannot: did the crawler arrive, and did it get a 200 when it did. Ours spent fifteen days failing that second half, and the fix was not submission volume.

    We read the numbers from the Bing Webmaster API every day on our own site. Fifteen consecutive days, 2026-11-08 to 11-22:.

    Three things to read out of it.

    Sources indicate that on 11-12 Bing fetched five URLs and got zero successful pages. On 11-18, 19 and 20 it fetched one, one and three, and still zero. If you only look at CrawledPages, you conclude Bing is working. Code2xx indicates it was being sent to addresses that redirect.

    That single 301 column on every one of the fifteen days is the fingerprint: one URL keeps being requested that answers with a redirect — usually the http twin, the bare host, or the path without its trailing slash. Our sitemap lists only the slashed, https, canonical form, which is why every fresh fetch had to be re-routed before anything could be read.

    Nothing we did to the site. We did not add pages, rewrite content, or increase submissions in that window. What appeared in the same 24 hours as the 0 → 4 in Code2xx was InLinks: 0 → 4.

    That is consistent with the explanation Bing's own documentation implies: crawl budget follows links. It is one observation on one property, so we are not going to turn it into a rule — but it does explain why "submit more URLs" produced nothing for two weeks.

    One caveat, because it is the same site: Bing improving did not mean the site was healthy. On the Google side the same 56 URLs went from 37 indexed to 13 in three days, with no change to the pages and no drop in crawl volume. We publish that series with the per-URL readings and a CSV at our index decay dataset — "the crawler came" and "the page was kept" are two different measurements, and only one of them was going well.

    The longer write-up, including the redirect variants that eat the fetches, is at Bing not indexing my site.

    According to recent reports, this is a write-up of how a set of static calculator pages computes the liquidation price of an isolated-margin USDT perpetual position for three exchanges (OKX, Bybit and MEXC), and how one function now produces both the numbers baked into the HTML at build time and the numbers the page script shows after a user types. The formulas are short. The bugs came from copying them.

    Every exchange documents roughly the same idea: a position is liquidated when its remaining margin falls to the maintenance margin. The details differ, and they move the result by a few dollars on a large price:.

    With entry price E, quantity q (notional / entry), leverage L, maintenance margin rate mmr, taker fee taker and extra margin extra, the long and short cases are:.

    For a 10,000 USDT position at 74,000 with 10x leverage, a 0.5% maintenance rate and each venue's regular taker rate (0.05%, 0.055%, 0.04%), this gives:.

    The spread is small, which is exactly why it went unnoticed.

    Recent findings suggest that the site grew one page at a time. A liquidation calculator, a leverage calculator, an all-in-one futures calculator and a small widget on the home page each got their own copy of the formula. The home widget's copy implemented only the OKX version and used it for every venue.

    Recent findings suggest that the result: the home page showed 66,971.69 for a Bybit long (the OKX formula with Bybit's 0.055% taker fee), while the dedicated calculator showed 66,934.67 for the same inputs. Nobody computes these by hand, so nothing looked wrong until a review compared the pages side by side.

    A second problem sat next to it: the widget's HTML contained numbers written in by hand for the first render. Before the script ran, every domain demonstrated figures calculated for one venue, including domains that do not cover that venue at all.

    The home widget now has a single function that returns display strings. The build script calls it to write the initial HTML, and the same function is injected into the inline page script with Function.prototype.toString():.

    With no extra margin, the general formulas reduce to these forms (q cancels out), so the widget and the full calculators agree to the cent. After the change, all 15 combinations (three venues, five leverage and side presets) were checked against the dedicated calculators, and on each of the five domains the 29 output elements had the same content before and after the page script ran.

    toString() has rules that are easy to break:.

    Sources indicate that not every page uses the serialized function yet. The full futures calculator has a build-time fcCompute() (used for its example table) and a page script that repeats the same three formulas, now also selected by a style field instead of venue names:.

    Those copies are kept in step by a comment in each file and by a reference value: 100,000 entry, 10x, 0.5% maintenance and 0.05% taker must give 90,497.74 on every page that uses the fee-in-denominator style. Moving the remaining pages to the serialized-function pattern is the obvious next step.

    Sources indicate that A copy can also drift by venue rather than by math. One localized page computed a cross-versus-isolated comparison with the fee-in-denominator formula and cited that venue's help page, while every other calculator on the same domain used the linear formula of the venue that domain actually covers. The two pages disagreed on the same trade. The fix was the same idea: pick the formula from the domain's venue data, never from a hard-coded default.

    #137933. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3838 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3838 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
    • According to recent reports, models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
    • It has been revealed that take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

    According to recent reports, models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

    It has been revealed that take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

    Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

    Sources indicate that we leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

    Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

    Sources indicate that for this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

    RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

    This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

    Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

    It has been revealed that we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

    In a recent development, A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

    In a recent development, each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

    858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

    A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

    Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below demonstrates how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

    Sources indicate that qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

    Sources indicate that this example demonstrates how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

    The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

    Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

    The figure below demonstrates how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

    Industry observers note that harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below highlights what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

    We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

    For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

    According to recent reports, to obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

    The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which revealed that 0.1 worked best).

    We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then indicated signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

    Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below highlights the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

    As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

    It has been revealed that the final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

    Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

    In a recent development, we also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

    Sources indicate that the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

    Industry observers note that merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

    Sources indicate that we started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

    Recent findings suggest that we concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

    Sources indicate that the plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

    Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

    Recent findings suggest that "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

    With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

    Industry observers note that despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

    Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

    Sources indicate that the super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

    The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

    This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

    Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

    During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets upcoming tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

    According to recent reports, on the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

    This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

    According to recent reports, we evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

    According to recent reports, every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

    For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

    For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

    Industry observers note that all three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

    Industry observers note that the adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

    To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

    Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

    What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

    We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

    Industry observers note that results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

    We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

    This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

    Industry observers note that this phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

    Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

    It has been revealed that however this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

    Sources indicate that throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

    In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

    According to recent reports, we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that you can get a Windows virtual machine for free and stay within the license terms, but every route is limited in time or credit.
    • This guide is for students who need Windows to practice administration or test software, and for IT staff who need a disposable lab.
    • Sources indicate that the key point: none of these gives you a permanent free Windows license.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that you can get a Windows virtual machine for free and stay within the license terms, but every route is limited in time or credit. Download a Microsoft evaluation ISO and run it in Hyper-V or VirtualBox, use Windows Sandbox for throwaway tests, or use free cloud credit on Azure. Pick by what you need the VM for, and set shutdown and budget limits so a free trial does not turn into a bill.

    This guide is for students who need Windows to practice administration or test software, and for IT staff who need a disposable lab. At the end you will know which legal route fits your computer, how to switch it on, how long it lasts, and what can cost money. It does not cover activating a normal Windows install or any key-sharing tricks.

    Sources indicate that the key point: none of these gives you a permanent free Windows license. A free VM runs software that you already have a license for, or an evaluation that expires.

    The Microsoft Evaluation Center is the most direct legal route and works offline once downloaded.

    Recent findings suggest that on 2026-11-23 the evaluation page listed "Windows 11 Enterprise, version 26H2" as an x64 ISO and an Arm64 ISO, plus "Windows 11 Enterprise LTSC 2024" as an x64 ISO. Microsoft describes it as "the full-featured software for a 90-day evaluation" and states a product key is not required. You register to download, and Windows prompts you to activate after installation with a Microsoft account.

    Know the end state before you start. Microsoft's page claims that if you do not activate or the evaluation expires, the desktop background turns black, a notice says the system is not genuine, and the PC shuts down every hour. It also says installing from the ISO cannot be uninstalled and the recovery partition cannot restore a previous Windows, so install it in a VM, not on your main computer.

    It has been revealed that the Windows Server 2025 evaluation page said on 2026-11-23 that the edition expires in 180 days. It offers a 64-bit ISO, a 64-bit VHD, and pre-built images on Azure. The ISO covers Datacenter and Standard, each as Server Core or Server with Desktop Experience. The VHD is English only. Evaluation versions must be activated over the internet in the first 10 days or they shut down automatically.

    Use the VHD with Hyper-V Generation 1 or the ISO if you want to practice the install. If you only need a lab for Active Directory or Group Policy practice, this is the better choice because 180 days covers a full semester.

    It has been revealed that microsoft used to publish ready-made Windows 11 development virtual machines on a developer download page. On 2026-11-23, that old address redirected to the general Windows developer tools page on Microsoft Learn, and that page did not list any VM images. We could not confirm that the images are right now offered, so use the evaluation ISO instead and treat any site that claims to offer them with caution.

    Hyper-V is built into Windows as an optional feature; there is nothing to download. Microsoft lists these requirements: Windows 10 or 11 Pro or Enterprise, a 64-bit processor with Second Level Address Translation (SLAT), CPU support for VM Monitor Mode Extension, and at least 4 GB of memory. The Hyper-V role cannot be installed on Windows 10 Home or Windows 11 Home.

    Open PowerShell as Administrator, because Microsoft states the commands fail otherwise:.

    Industry observers note that enter Y to restart. DISM does the same job:.

    Microsoft says you should see "The operation completed successfully." The graphical route on Windows 11 is Control Panel, Programs, Programs and Features, Turn Windows Features on or off, then select Hyper-V and OK.

    After the restart, open Hyper-V Manager, choose Upcoming, then Virtual Machine, and point the installation media at the evaluation ISO. Give a Windows 11 VM at least 4 GB of memory and 2 virtual processors if your computer has the room; Windows 11 itself has its own hardware requirements, so check them on Microsoft's device specifications page.

    Sources indicate that microsoft warns that third-party virtualization apps such as VMware Workstation and VirtualBox rely on processor features Hyper-V also needs. You can install both, but if you start a VM in the other app while the Hyper-V hypervisor is running, the VM might not start or might run unreliably. Pick one for each work session.

    Windows Sandbox is a disposable, lightweight desktop. It is not for keeping files or installing a lab; it is for opening something risky once and throwing it away.

    Sources indicate that microsoft lists the prerequisites: AMD64 or Arm64 architecture, virtualization enabled in the BIOS, at least 4 GB of RAM (8 GB recommended), at least 1 GB of free disk space and at least two CPU cores. To turn it on, search for "Turn Windows Features on or off," select Windows Sandbox, select OK and restart if prompted. From an elevated PowerShell prompt, the equivalent is:.

    In a recent development, if the Windows Sandbox option is missing, Microsoft says your computer does not meet the requirements. Also note that beginning in Windows 11 version 24H2, inbox store apps such as Calculator, Photos, Notepad and Terminal are not available inside it.

    VirtualBox is free third-party virtualization software that runs on Windows Home as well, which Hyper-V cannot. It does not supply a Windows license, so install an evaluation ISO or a Windows version you already own. We did not verify VirtualBox's current version or extension license terms in this run; check the VirtualBox downloads page and its license text before using it at work.

    A cloud VM saves your PC's memory and is reachable from anywhere, but it is the route that can produce a bill.

    According to recent reports, the Azure free account page on 2026-11-23 offered a "$200 credit" to use on Azure services within 30 days. You must move to pay-as-you-go within 30 days or after using the credit, whichever comes first, to keep services running. New customers also get "750 hours each of B1s, B2pts v2 (Arm-based), and B2ats v2 (AMD-based) burstable VMs" for 12 months. That wording covers specific burstable B-series sizes; the page does not say it covers every Windows VM, so check the size and the price in the portal before you create it. A non-prepaid credit or debit card is required, and you may see a one-dollar verification hold.

    The Azure for Students page highlighted a "$100 credit" to use within 12 months, renewable annually while you remain a student, with "No credit card required." It is for full-time university students signing up with a school email, one account per person. For classroom practice this is usually the safer route because there is no card to be charged by accident.

    Do these before you leave a cloud VM running:.

    Recent findings suggest that AWS changed its free tier to a credit-based model. The AWS Free Tier page on 2026-11-23 noted fresh accounts receive $100 immediately and can earn up to $100 more by exploring services, up to $200 in total, and that the account closes six months after opening or when credits run out, whichever comes first. The free plan is limited to select services; the page did not say which EC2 instance types are eligible, so check the console before launching Windows, which carries a license charge in AWS pricing.

    Recent findings suggest that google Cloud's free trial gives "$300 in free Welcome credit which is valid for 90 days," but the documentation lists creating VM instances based on Windows Server among the things the free trial does not allow. For a Windows VM, Azure is the better cloud fit. Our free tier comparison covers the three platforms side by side.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
    • In a recent development, could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
    • Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

    In a recent development, could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

    Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

    Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

    Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

    The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

    Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, noted:.

    “Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

    According to recent reports, because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”.

    The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

    Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

    Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

    Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

    Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

    The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

    Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

    The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

    Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

    #137928. Latest Update: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2444 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model.
    • In a recent development, inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
    • We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

    In a recent development, inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

    We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

    This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

    According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

    Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

    It has been revealed that architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

    In a recent development, text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

    In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

    Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

    Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

    In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

    We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

    You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

    #137926. Tech Report: cPanel to Microsoft 365 Migration: Step-by-Step, MX Cutover Included

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1923 w)
